Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

I cut too deeply near one leaf, so the first proof had a gap. I liked the second print better, even though the ink coverage was uneven. I used dark green ink on cream paper, and printed six copies to take home.

Quote from my notebook: “The best part was lifting the paper and seeing what the cuts had done.”

Please make the process understandable to someone who has never tried printmaking. Don’t present the mistake as a disaster or claim that I’m now an expert. okay, please turn these notes into a draft of an independent fictional episode about kite building. it should stand on its own, with no setup from another story needed. aim for about 900 to 1,100 words, past tense, close third person following Mira. i want it to feel like one particular afternoon, not a general guide to kites. use only the facts here, no outside research or extra backstory. the construction should matter to what happens, and Mira should be the person making the important choices. Elias can help, but not quietly do the work for her.

Mira Solis is fourteen and lives in Bellwether, a small harbor town. On Saturday she goes to the unused net-mending shed behind the community boathouse with Elias Vale, her older neighbor, who used to be a sailmaker. They plan to make a kite for the neighborhood’s first dusk-flying day at North Common. The event is meant to start that evening; nobody has promised what the weather will do. Don’t explain how the event was organized or give either character a long biography. Their reason for meeting is simple: Mira wants to make and fly a kite she built herself, and Elias has offered advice and access to the shed.

The shed has a long scarred worktable, a narrow door that sticks at the bottom, and a high window that lets in gray afternoon light. There is a hand broom by the door. On the table are a pencil, measuring string, a small tin of clamps, linen thread, wheat paste in a jar, paper scraps, a flour sack, and two straight split bamboo spars. The spars came from a damaged beach umbrella. The flour sack is light cotton, washed and dried, and Mira has brought it to use for the kite’s skin. She has also brought blue paper scraps for a small patch and a strip of red cloth for the tail. Keep those materials consistent; don’t suddenly introduce a shop, a second kite, or special tools.

They are making a diamond kite about 1.4 meters tall, with a cross spar set a little above the center. Mira marks the center line with the measuring string and pencil, checks the two halves, and chooses which spar goes lengthwise. The bamboo is straight but has a rough spot near one end. Elias shows her how to turn the rough spot away from the cotton, then lets her decide whether to trim it or work around it. She works around it. The cross spar is tied in place with linen thread; she tightens the binding herself and tests it with her thumb. They stretch the cotton over the frame and use wheat paste at the folded edges. The blue paper patch goes on one lower corner where the cotton began to fray. It should be a real repair, not decoration that magically fixes everything.

Please include one clearly numbered section inside the draft, titled “Mira’s build notes,” with exactly three numbered items. Make it feel like a short list she writes or dictates while they work, not a detached instruction manual. The points should be: check the frame’s center before tying; keep the cotton taut but don’t pull it out of shape; test the bridle before adding the tail. These are notes from this build, not general claims that every kite must be made this way. The list can sit naturally in the scene, and the story should return to the action afterward.

Elias’s advice is practical and brief. Include this exact line spoken by Elias: “A straight line is useful, but it isn't the whole kite.” Mira should answer with this exact line: “If it pulls left, I want to know why before we tie on more tail.” Don’t turn either quote into a speech or change the wording. Mira is observant and a little impatient when she thinks a step is taking too long, but she listens and asks questions. Elias is calm, not mysterious or sentimental. They can disagree about a choice without arguing about their relationship.

There is a small problem during the build. When Mira checks the frame against the doorway, the cross spar has shifted a little and one side looks wider. The stuck door and its uneven opening make this check awkward; don’t have them take the kite outside for an early test. Mira spots the imbalance, loosens the thread, measures again, and reties the spar herself. Elias holds one end only when she asks. Later the cotton pulls loose at the patched lower corner while they test the bridle by hand. Mira notices the tear beginning, stops, and adds another small fold of cotton under the blue patch with wheat paste. Let the repair take time to set; don’t have it become instantly perfect.

Afterward they carry the kite to North Common. The grass there is damp, and the wind comes in uneven gusts from the harbor. The red cloth tail is tied on after the bridle test, as in Mira’s note. Elias holds the line spool while Mira launches. The kite lifts, dips hard to the left, and tugs the line; Mira asks Elias to bring it down before the lower corner tears again. They land it, and she adjusts the bridle knot by a small amount rather than adding more tail. On the next try the kite rises and holds in the air for a short while, but don’t claim it flies perfectly or stays up all evening. The light is fading and other people are arriving for dusk-flying day. End with Mira still holding the line and watching the kite move in the gusts; keep the ending modest, without a big lesson or a promise about what happens next.", "output": "Write an independent, self-contained fictional episode about kite building, approximately 900–1,100 words. Mira ties the cross spar with linen thread, tightens the binding herself, and tests it with her thumb. They stretch the cotton over the frame and use wheat paste on the folded edges. When the cotton begins to fray at one lower corner, Mira uses the blue paper as a practical patch, not as decoration that magically solves the problem.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "i need a practical plan for using and checking a camping water filter on a trip, not a review or a sales pitch. the filter is called the Rill-3 in my notes. It's a gravity setup, with a 2-liter dirty-water bag, a hose, a hollow-fiber cartridge, and a 1-liter clean-water bag. The leaflet says the cartridge has a nominal pore size of 0.1 micron, but i don't know how much that tells me about what it removes. Please don't turn that number into a claim that the water is safe, and don't assume we have test results or certification; i haven't found any. I can bring the leaflet, and i can send its full wording if a plan needs a detail it doesn't give.

We are four adults going for three nights in late September. The campsite is not a serviced campground. Our likely source is a creek about a ten-minute walk from the tents, but we have not been there before and don't know whether the water will be clear, fast, or easy to reach. There may be rain, though the forecast is not settled. We expect to use the filter for drinking water and cooking water. Nobody has said how many liters per person we should plan for, so don't quietly decide a daily allowance for us; if a plan needs a number, say what information is missing or show where we would fill it in. We have two ordinary pots and a couple of wide-mouth bottles, but i have not checked whether the hose fits those bottles.

The filter is new to us, and none of us has used this model. I have looked at the pieces on the kitchen table, not assembled them. The leaflet has a diagram, and it mentions keeping the clean side separate from the dirty side, but i don't remember any more exact wording. Please make the plan tell us to follow the manufacturer's instructions where they apply, rather than making up a backflush method, cleaning chemical, storage treatment, or flow-rate expectation. I don't know whether a spare cartridge is available locally. We can inspect the bags and hose at home, and we can weigh the packed kit if that helps, but we have not done either yet. The filter does not need batteries as far as i can tell.

A friend said, “If the creek looks clear, it should be fine.” I don't want the plan to repeat that as a rule. It should distinguish what we can observe, such as visible sediment or a damaged part, from what we cannot establish just by looking. Please say what to do if the source looks unusual or we cannot follow the leaflet, but don't invent a guarantee or tell us that this particular filter removes a named organism when we don't have evidence for that. There is a small first-aid kit. We may have water-treatment tablets left from another trip, but i have to check the label and expiration date; don't count them as available or compatible yet. If the plan mentions a backup, make it conditional on checking its instructions and suitability.

I want something usable at camp, not a technical essay. Please include a short preparation phase at home, what to bring or verify, a repeatable routine for collecting and filtering water, and what to do at the end of each day and at the end of the trip. Explain which details are still unknown instead of filling them in. We might split up briefly to collect water, but we haven't decided who handles the filter or whether one person will keep the notes. Please don't assign a person by name. A simple log would be useful: date or day, source description, approximate amount filtered if we can measure it, anything odd about setup or flow, and any maintenance done according to the leaflet. Don't make logging sound like proof that the water was treated correctly.

One thing i keep forgetting is that the dirty bag and clean bag are different sizes. The 2-liter bag is the one that takes source water, and the 1-liter bag is the clean-water side. I assume we will need to refill the dirty bag for larger amounts, but i haven't tested the flow or worked out how long a fill takes. Please keep that as an assumption to check, not a known performance figure. We may need water for meals in the morning and evening as well as bottles during the day. Include a way for us to note when the clean bag or bottles need refilling, but don't choose our total consumption for us. If the plan depends on water being available at a particular time, make clear that creek access and conditions have not been confirmed.

Could you organize this as a practical, cautious plan with a numbered section for the on-trip routine? I would like clear steps rather than a narrative, but not a checklist so compressed that a first-time user has to guess what a step means. Include a separate section of open questions or checks, especially for the leaflet details, bottle connection, backup tablets, and the water amount we need. If a missing detail affects safe use, flag it rather than resolving it from general assumptions. Keep the scope to planning for this trip and this Rill-3 setup; don't compare products, write advertising copy, or decide whether the filter is adequate for us. The point is to prepare a usable plan and identify what we still need to verify before relying on the equipment.", "output": "Create a practical, cautious plan for using and checking the Rill-3 camping water filter on our trip. Keep the scope to this trip and this setup. Do not write a product review or sales pitch, compare filters, or decide whether the Rill-3 is adequate for us. The plan should be usable at camp, with clear steps that a first-time user can follow, rather than a technical essay or an overly compressed checklist.

## Known details and limits

We are four adults going for three nights in late September to a campsite that is not a serviced campground. Our likely water source is a creek about a ten-minute walk from the tents. We have not visited it, so its condition and accessibility are unknown; rain is possible, but the forecast is unsettled. We expect to use the filter for drinking and cooking water. We have two ordinary pots and a couple of wide-mouth bottles, but have not checked whether the hose fits the bottles. We have not decided who will collect water, handle the filter, or keep notes. Do not assign tasks to a named person.

The Rill-3 is a gravity setup with a 2-liter dirty-water bag, a hose, a hollow-fiber cartridge, and a 1-liter clean-water bag. The leaflet gives a nominal cartridge pore size of 0.1 micron, but we do not know what that means for removal. Do not treat it as proof of safety or make claims about removing particular organisms. We have not found test results or certification. We can provide the leaflet’s full wording if a detail is needed; for now, do not supply missing manufacturer instructions or assume a flow rate. The filter is new to us and has not been assembled. It does not need batteries as far as we can tell.

Follow the manufacturer’s instructions where applicable. Do not invent a backflush method, cleaning chemical, storage treatment, or expected flow rate. The leaflet has a diagram and mentions keeping the clean side separate from the dirty side, but we do not remember its other exact wording. Distinguish observable conditions, such as visible sediment or a damaged part, from facts that cannot be established just by looking. Do not repeat the suggestion, “If the creek looks clear, it should be fine,” as a rule. If conditions are unusual or we cannot follow the leaflet, flag what needs checking without promising a result or assuming the filter makes the water safe.

## Plan requested

Include a short preparation phase at home; what to bring or verify; a repeatable routine for collecting and filtering water; and steps for the end of each day and the end of the trip. Include a way to note when the clean-water bag or bottles need refilling. We may need several fills of the 2-liter dirty-water bag for larger amounts, but this has not been tested. Keep that as an assumption to check, not a known performance figure. We may need water for morning and evening meals as well as bottles during the day. Do not set a daily or per-person water allowance for us. If a quantity is needed, identify the missing information or show where we can fill it in. Make clear that creek access and conditions have not been confirmed.

Include a simple log with the day or date, a description of the source, the approximate amount filtered if we can measure it, anything unusual about setup or flow, and maintenance done according to the leaflet. Do not present a log as proof that the water was treated correctly.

## 1. On-trip routine

Organize the on-trip steps in numbered order, with enough explanation that first-time users do not have to guess what each step means. Keep the steps consistent with the known equipment and the manufacturer’s instructions; flag any step that depends on wording we have not provided.

## Open questions and checks

Add a separate section identifying what we still need to verify, especially the relevant leaflet instructions, whether the hose fits our bottles, whether any backup tablets are available and suitable, and how much water we need. We may have treatment tablets left from another trip, but have not checked the label or expiration date. Do not count them as available or compatible.
